analysis.one_liner: Bars oil refiners from charging independent gas stations more wholesale than their own stores pay effectively, with fines and lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 137 bipartisan cosponsors and was approved by a subcommittee, but never received a vote in the full House committee or on the floor, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for a refiner to sell gasoline to a station owner for resale at a price higher than what the refiner effectively charges itself at its own company-run stations, after accounting for the station's operating costs. It would also ban refiners from striking deals to dictate the maximum retail price at independent stations. Enforcement would come through federal fines, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits with triple damages, jury trials, and attorney fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent and franchised gasoline station dealers, who buy fuel under refiner brand names. The bill gives them a price benchmark and a private right of action, so a refiner squeezing its dealers with above-market wholesale prices could be sued and fined. Consumers benefit indirectly: if wholesale prices paid by independent stations track the refiner's own retail economics, dealers can compete on price instead of being outcompeted by refiner-run stations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Independent gas station dealers and drivers

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a refiner to sell motor fuel to any customer for resale at a price higher than the refiner's adjusted retail price for the same grade of fuel at its own company-operated outlet in the same area [S2][S3].
Prohibits refiners from entering any scheme or agreement to set or maintain maximum retail prices of motor fuel, except at their own direct-operated outlets [S2][S3].

Lets injured parties sue as individuals or in class actions, recover the greater of treble damages or $5,000 per violation plus attorneys' fees, with a right to jury trial, and lets state attorneys general sue on residents' behalf with penalties of $1,000 to $25,000 per violation [S2][S3].

Eases the plaintiff's burden by allowing a prima facie case on showing the refiner sold fuel above 94 percent of its own retail price (90 percent for branded wholesalers), with the refiner bearing the burden of rebuttal [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners, including major integrated oil companies. They face federal and state fines for each violation, treble-damages class actions from dealers, and restrictions on the wholesale and resale pricing arrangements they use to structure their dealer networks. Compliance and litigation costs could be passed into fuel prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil refiners and major oil companies

drawbacks.text: The bill is a form of price regulation: pegging wholesale prices to a refiner's own retail margins, with penalties of up to $25,000 per violation and treble damages, could push refiners to supply fewer independent dealers and convert stations to company operation, the opposite of the bill's aim [S3].

Bright-line tests (94 percent or 90 percent of the refiner's retail price) may misjudge real costs, since operating expenses vary by station and state; the bill addresses this with surveys and rebuttals but still creates litigation over contested expense figures [S2][S3].

A good-faith critic would note that restricting refiner pricing agreements with dealers can limit pricing flexibility that sometimes holds retail prices down, and enforcement costs could ultimately show up in what consumers pay at the pump [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem — refiners that own both the wholesale and retail levels of the market could price independent dealers out while favoring their own stations. The remedy is aggressive, using bright-line price tests, private class actions, and stacked federal and state fines, which carries a genuine risk of over-enforcement and fewer independent dealers. But the design (rebutable presumptions, state-level cost surveys, fee-shifting) shows an attempt to balance that. The main cost is borne by refiners; the main uncertainty is whether consumers or just dealers capture the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees for the whole Congress; a subcommittee held hearings, marked it up, and sent it to the full committee in August 1992, but the full committee never acted and it never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Introduced July 22, 1991 by Rep. Mike Synar with 137 cosponsors, split 92 Democrats and 45 Republicans [S4][S5].
Referred jointly to the Committees on Energy and Commerce and Judiciary on July 22, 1991, then to subcommittees in each [S5].
A subcommittee held hearings on June 11, 1992, and on August 11, 1992 marked the bill up and forwarded it to the full Energy and Commerce Committee [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a vote in the full committee or on the House floor, and expired when the 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil refiners benefit, because the restrictions on their wholesale and resale pricing never took effect. Independent dealers and consumers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was strongly bipartisan — 92 of 267 House Democrats and 45 of 167 House Republicans signed on — so the bill's death in committee was not a party-line result.

industries.industry: Oil refiners and major oil companies
industries.note: The bill exposes refiners to federal and state fines per violation and treble-damages class actions if they sell wholesale fuel above their own adjusted retail price or dictate dealers' maximum retail prices. Their interest in the bill runs against dealers and potentially consumers, since the arrangement being restricted lets refiners favor their own stations.

industries.industry: Independent and branded gasoline station dealers
industries.note: Dealers gain a price benchmark tied to the refiner's own retail economics plus a private right of action with fee-shifting, letting them challenge wholesale prices that squeeze their margins. They are small-business owners, so their gain aligns with keeping independent retail competition alive.

industries.industry: Consumers of gasoline and diesel fuel
industries.note: If the rule keeps independent stations price-competitive, retail fuel prices could face more competition, but enforcement costs and reduced refiner pricing flexibility could push pump prices up. The direct beneficiaries are dealers; consumer benefit is indirect.
